SearchAliases: Complete Command of the Precious Mirror
Senses.Explanation: The transmitted Precious Mirror complete command is the guiding matter that Dongshan Liangjie says he received from Yunyan Tansheng and entrusted to Caoshan Benji. In this use, 寶鏡三昧 names what is received or handed on rather than the title heading itself. Dongshan says, “I personally received the Precious Mirror complete command from my former teacher Yunyan; its matter exhausts the essential point; now I entrust it to you” (吾在雲巖先師處親印寶鏡三昧。事窮的要。今付于汝). Juelang Daosheng likewise calls it the guiding matter (宗旨) that Caoshan personally received from Dongshan. An unnamed monk can also ask what 寶鏡三昧 is and receive an answer, showing the name used for the transmitted matter rather than merely cited as a book title. Liangting Jingting says Dongshan orally proclaimed it to Caoshan but challenges the inference that Yunyan supplied its exact wording. The transmission is therefore attested, while authorship of the titled text remains uncertain.

Senses.Explanation: Precious Mirror Complete Command is also the title of a verse or text. Later sources print that title under Dongshan Liangjie's name, but their own historical comments leave composition uncertain. Yongjue Yuanxian calls 寶鏡三昧 a book privately transmitted by Dongshan Liangjie to Caoshan Benji. He then argues that Dongshan's statement about receiving it from Yunyan means Dongshan did not compose it, proposes Yunyan as author, reports another account involving Yaoshan, and concludes that the earlier history cannot now be verified. Drafts from Chan Master Weilin's Traveling Hermitage prints the verse beneath the heading “Dongshan Liangjie, Precious Mirror Complete Command,” but an editorial heading establishes the title and traditional placement, not authorship. This title sense therefore remains distinct from passages where 寶鏡三昧 means the complete command or guiding matter being received and entrusted.

Senses.Explanation: The (延壽堂), literally 'hall for extending life,' is the monastery infirmary where sick monastics are housed and tended. Rulebooks list its supervisor among the communal offices and describe appointing a conscientious person; Mingjue Cong recounts spending three months there with a grave illness, while Langting Jingting raises the case of an unnamed monk who dies in the hall. The auspicious name does not turn it into a longevity shrine.
